summaries.example: Think about a wooden chair. You can ask, “Does the chair exist?” and also, “What makes it a chair?” The first question is about its existence. The second is about its essence, or what it is. Ibn Sina says these questions are connected, but they are not the same. A chair could be imagined even when no real chair is nearby.
summaries.summary: Ibn Sina’s metaphysics asks the biggest questions about reality. He calls it a science of being: the study of everything that exists, considered as existing. It is also connected to theology because it asks whether there is a first principle that does not depend on anything else. Ibn Sina separates a thing’s essence—what it is—from its existence—the fact that it is. Most things are possible in themselves: they could exist or fail to exist, so they need causes. The first principle is necessary in itself, unique, simple, and uncaused. Ibn Sina says this principle causes the world through a timeless flow called emanation. In this picture, metaphysics helps explain the world, nature, minds, and other areas of knowledge.
key_ideas: Ibn Sina, also called Avicenna, treats metaphysics as a careful science about being itself, not just about one kind of thing.
Metaphysics studies all beings together, while also asking whether there is a first, uncaused principle.
For most things, what a thing is and the fact that it exists are different. The first principle is different because it is necessary existence itself.
Things that are possible need causes. Ibn Sina says the chain of causes ultimately depends on one necessary first principle.
Ibn Sina describes the world as created by this principle without a beginning in time, and explains its order through emanation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ibn Sina gives us a powerful way to sort out questions that people often mix together: What is a thing? Does it exist? Why does it exist? His ideas also show how philosophy, science, and theology can be connected in a large system. They influenced later thinkers in both Islamic philosophy and medieval European philosophy.

important_terms.definition: The study of what it means for things to be and how all beings fit together.
The fact that something is real, either outside the mind or as something imagined or understood in the mind.
What a thing is—its basic nature or answer to the question “What is it?”
Something that can exist but does not have to exist. It depends on a cause to be real.
Something that must exist and does not depend on another cause for its existence.
A reason or source that helps explain why something exists or happens.
The idea that beings flow or come from a first source in a timeless order.

questions_to_think_about: Can you imagine something that does not exist in the room? Does it exist in any sense?
Is knowing what something is the same as knowing that it exists?
Why might a chain of causes need a first cause?
Can something be eternal and still depend on a cause?

summaries.example: Consider the triangle. Its essence is the structure described by “three-sided polygon.” That description alone does not place a triangle on a particular page or in the physical world. A drawn triangle has concrete existence; a triangle understood by the mind has mental existence. Ibn Sina uses this kind of distinction to argue that, for ordinary things, knowing what something is does not by itself prove that it exists. Their possible essences require a cause to be actual.
summaries.summary: Ibn Sina defines metaphysics as the science of the existent precisely as existent. This makes it universal: unlike physics or another specialized science, it does not investigate only one region of reality. Yet metaphysics also has a theological task, because it must establish the First Principle and determine its properties. The apparent tension is resolved through two ways of considering being. Being taken without a special condition is common to all beings; being considered as the being of the First Principle is uncaused and necessary. In ordinary beings, essence or quiddity is distinct from existence. Their essences are possible in themselves, and their existence is received through causes. The First Principle has no distinct essence added to existence: it is necessary existence itself. Ibn Sina therefore argues for a unique, simple first cause. His account of creation is not temporal beginning but an eternal dependence of the world on its first cause. Through emanation, the first principle’s intellectual activity explains the ordered derivation of intelligences, souls, celestial bodies, and the sublunary world. This metaphysical structure supports accounts of nature, intellect, prophecy, and the problem of evil.
key_ideas: Metaphysics has a dual character: its subject is being as such, making it ontology; its central investigation establishes the First Principle, making it theology.

Being is predicated of both the First Principle and caused things, but not in exactly the same mode. The Principle is necessary in itself; other things are possible in themselves and necessary through a cause.
Essence and existence are distinct in caused beings. This is an ontological distinction, not merely a difference between two words or concepts.
Quiddity is neither universal nor particular in itself. It can occur in a particular external thing or be considered universally in the mind.
Ibn Sina’s causal reasoning leads to a unique, simple, uncaused principle. A causal series cannot explain its members without a first cause outside the series.
Creation is an atemporal dependence of the world on its cause. Thus the world may be eternal in motion while still being absolutely caused or “instaured.”
summaries.why_it_matters: Ibn Sina’s analysis became central to later debates about existence, essence, causation, divine simplicity, and the relation between philosophy and theology. It also offers a model of systematic philosophy: questions about ordinary objects, possibility, and causation lead toward a theory of the whole of reality. Studying his distinctions helps explain why medieval philosophers asked not only whether something exists, but in what way and through what dependence it exists.

important_terms.definition: For Ibn Sina, the rational discipline that studies the existent as existent and seeks an account of reality as a whole.
The study of being or existence, especially the general features shared by beings.
The part of metaphysics that investigates the First Principle and establishes its existence and attributes.
A thing’s “whatness”: the nature or answer to the question of what it is, considered apart from an assertion that it exists.
The fact or actuality of being. Ibn Sina distinguishes mental existence from existence in concrete things.
That which is dependent and could either exist or not exist when considered in itself.
That which exists through itself, without a cause; Ibn Sina identifies it as the unique First Principle.
The dependence relation by which a possible thing is made necessary through something else.

questions_to_think_about: If a definition tells us what something is, why might it fail to show that the thing exists?
Does saying that being applies to God and creatures make their existence identical, or can existence have different modes?
Can an eternal effect still depend on a cause? What would “priority” mean if it is not temporal?
Does the distinction between essence and existence support a proof of a first principle?
What problems arise when mental objects are said to have a kind of existence?

summaries.example: Suppose you design a video-game dragon. You can describe what a dragon is in the game—its shape, abilities, and rules—even before the dragon appears on the screen. That description is like an essence. The dragon’s appearance in the game is like existence in a particular setting. Ibn Sina says that for many things, knowing the description does not prove that the thing is real. Something else must explain why it exists.
summaries.summary: Ibn Sina presents metaphysics as the most universal science because it studies being itself rather than one limited group of objects. It is also theological in a specific sense: it must establish the existence and features of a First Principle. These two jobs fit together. Being can be considered generally, without adding a special condition, or it can be considered as the being of the uncaused principle. For ordinary things, essence and existence are distinct. A thing may be understandable as a kind of thing without actually existing, and if it does exist, its existence depends on a cause. Such things are possible in themselves but necessary through another. The First Principle is necessary in itself, unique, simple, and not dependent on a cause. Ibn Sina says that existence belongs to both the principle and its effects, but in different modes; this helps him avoid treating them as identical. His account of creation is also unusual: the world can be eternal and eternally moving while still depending on the First Principle in an atemporal way. Emanation describes how an ordered reality flows from that first source, with intelligences, souls, celestial bodies, and earthly things connected in a causal hierarchy.
key_ideas: Ibn Sina combines two traditional views of metaphysics. It studies being generally, but it also investigates the First Principle.
He distinguishes the question “What is this?” from “Does this exist?” A thing’s essence does not automatically guarantee its existence.
Most things are possible in themselves. They become necessary through a cause that makes them exist.
The First Principle is necessary in itself, uncaused, unique, simple, and not made of separate essence and existence.
Being applies to both the First Principle and the world, but existence is not expressed in exactly the same way in both. This is a qualified or modulated sameness.
Ibn Sina explains the world through timeless creation and emanation: reality depends continuously on the First Principle, while different levels of beings arise in an ordered way.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ibn Sina’s framework shows how a philosopher can connect abstract logic with questions about the universe. His distinctions influenced later discussions in Islamic, Jewish, and Christian philosophy, especially debates about whether existence is something added to an essence, how causes work, and how a first principle relates to a changing world. The entry also demonstrates that philosophical arguments can preserve important differences rather than forcing every viewpoint into a simple yes-or-no answer.

important_terms.definition: The study of being and reality as a whole. Ibn Sina sees it as the most universal science.
The study of beings simply as beings, including the features they share because they exist.
The study of the First Principle, including whether it exists and what follows from its existence.
The answer to “What is it?”—the nature or kind of a thing, considered apart from whether it is actually present.
The fact that something is, either in the world or in the mind as an imagined or understood object.
Something that could exist or not exist by itself, and therefore depends on a cause when it exists.
Something that cannot fail to exist and needs no cause outside itself.
The explanation of how one thing depends on another for its existence or condition.

questions_to_think_about: Can a clear description of something show that it exists? Why or why not?
What is the difference between something being possible by itself and being necessary because of a cause?
Why does Ibn Sina think two completely independent necessary beings could not both exist?
How can the world be eternal in motion yet still depend on a first cause?
Does calling metaphysics both ontology and theology make it broader than ordinary sciences?
